```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

projectData makes the objects in installed data packages available under the
names you expect, and reads each object only when you first use it. The normal
workflow has three steps:

1. **Install** the data package.
2. **Attach** it.
3. **Use** its objects, interactively or in a script.

Need another data package later? Attach it too. If the packages define the same
name, projectData asks you to decide which one you mean (see
[Conflicts](#conflicts)); it never picks a winner by order.

## 1. Install

Installing is ordinary R package installation and is not done by projectData. A
data package distributed as a tarball (for example from Zenodo) is installed
like any source package:

```r
install.packages("path/to/rnaseqData_1.0.0.tar.gz", repos = NULL, type = "source")
```

To keep this vignette offline, the next chunk builds two tiny throwaway data
packages in a temporary library. In real use, skip this chunk and omit the
`lib.loc` argument below.

```{r fixtures}
library(projectData)
source(system.file("examples", "fixtures.R", package = "projectData"))

lib <- fixture_library()
fixture_package(lib, "rnaseqData", "1.0.0", lazy = TRUE, datasets = list(
  counts_rna = list(counts_rna = matrix(1:6, 2)),
  meta_rna   = list(meta_rna = data.frame(sample = c("a", "b")))
))
fixture_package(lib, "proteinData", "2.1.0", lazy = FALSE, datasets = list(
  counts_prot = list(counts_prot = matrix(7:12, 2)),
  meta_prot   = list(meta_prot = data.frame(sample = c("a", "b")))
))
```

## 2. Attach

`data_attach()` takes the name of an installed data package. It records what
the package contains and puts its objects on the search path under their own
names. This reads package metadata only: no data values are read, and nothing is
installed. Nothing is attached unless you call this function.

```{r attach}
data_attach("rnaseqData", lib.loc = lib)
```

Use the 

## 3. Use

Use the objects by their ordinary names. The first use of an object reads it.

```{r use}
data_config(messages = TRUE)
counts_rna
```

The message says that local installed files were used and that nothing was
downloaded. The same code works in a script after the `data_attach()` call.

Attach another package whenever you need it. Objects already in use are not
affected.

```{r attach-second}
data_attach("proteinData", lib.loc = lib)
counts_prot
```

## Looking at what is attached

These read only recorded metadata. They never open any data.

```{r catalog}
data_catalog()[, c("collection", "exposed_name", "resource", "state")]
```

`state` is `unopened` until the object has been used, then `ready`. The
`resource` column is the loadable unit, which can differ from the object name.
A resource that produces several objects is opened once for all of them.

`data_info("counts_rna")` returns the full provenance row for a name: package,
version, installed location, source file, and how the mapping was determined.
`data_help("counts_rna")` opens the help page of the original topic in the
source package. It is separate from inspection and never runs implicitly.

## Getting objects explicitly

Bare names are convenient, but `data_get()` returns an object without relying on
what is on the search path, so it is the more robust choice inside functions
and scripts. (Attached bindings can also be evaluated by IDE completion or
previews; see `system.file("ide-repro", package = "projectData")`.)

```{r explicit}
data_get("meta_prot")
data_get("meta_rna", collection = "rnaseqData")
```

Give several names to open several objects in one call. This is a good way to
open large objects at the start of a batch job: the first-access messages
appear together, before the rest of the analysis runs.

```{r several}
str(data_get(c("meta_rna", "meta_prot")))
```

## Getting one object without attaching

Sometimes you want a single object and no new names on the search path, much as
you would write `package::object` for an exported object. Give `data_get()` the
`package`:

```{r get-unattached}
fixture_package(lib, "imagingData", "0.3.0", lazy = TRUE, datasets = list(
  counts_img = list(counts_img = matrix(13:18, 2))
))

counts_img <- data_get("counts_img", package = "imagingData", lib.loc = lib)
counts_img
"imagingData" %in% data_collections()$package[data_collections()$attached]
```

There is nothing to register first. `data_get()` inventories the package if
necessary (metadata only), then returns the object. It does not attach anything
and does not change collections that are already attached. The name is looked up
in that package itself, so preferences, primary collections and suffixes you set
for attached access do not affect it.

`data_get()` still **opens** the object you ask for; it is not a metadata query.
Use `data_catalog()` or `data_query()` to look without opening. If you attach the
package later, the object is not read again.

## First-access messages

Before each resource is read for the first time, projectData prints a message
naming the collection, the objects, the size of the source file when it is a
single file, and the loader. For large data this is the moment to notice what is
about to load. Turn the messages off with `data_config(messages = FALSE)`; the
setting lasts for the session.

## Looking at a package without attaching it

`data_query()` shows what a package contains, and which names would collide with
the packages you list or with what is already attached, **without attaching
anything or remembering anything**. Use it to look before you attach.

```{r query}
data_detach()

fixture_package(lib, "rnaseqBatch2", "1.0.0", lazy = TRUE, datasets = list(
  counts_rna = list(counts_rna = matrix(101:106, 2)),
  meta_rna   = list(meta_rna = data.frame(sample = c("c", "d")))
))

data_query(c("rnaseqData", "rnaseqBatch2"), lib.loc = lib,
           id = c("batch1", "batch2"))[, c("collection", "exposed_name", "binding")]
nrow(data_collections())
```

The query already shows the problem: `counts_rna` and `meta_rna` exist in both
packages, so their `binding` is `ambiguous`. The query changed nothing: no
collections are attached.

## Conflicts {#conflicts}

When two attached collections define the same name, the name projectData will never resolve the name
by order. Attaching still succeeds, and the catalog flags the conflict. Using the
bare name fails with an error that lists the candidates. Use `id` to give each
collection a name of your own:

```{r conflict, error = TRUE}
data_attach(c("rnaseqData", "rnaseqBatch2"), lib.loc = lib, id = c("batch1", "batch2"))
counts_rna
```

There are three ways to resolve conflicts, and they can be combined.

**Per-object preference.** Choose the collection for a particular name. This is
the right tool when an object from one package is always preferred over an object with the same name in another package:.

```{r prefer}
data_prefer("counts_rna", "batch1")
counts_rna
```

Other contested names stay unresolved until you decide them:

```{r prefer-others, error = TRUE}
meta_rna
```

**A primary collection.** If one collection should win *all* its contested
names, designate it. If an object is preferred from a non-primary collection, setting a per-object preference will override the primary designation. A primary collection can also be set when attaching:
`data_attach("rnaseqData", id = "batch1", primary = "batch1")`.

```{r primary}
data_primary("batch1")
meta_rna
```

**Suffix aliases and qualified access.**  Qualified access, `data_get(name, collection =)`, is the most robust way to access objects within scripts or functions.  This returns the value of the named object and also reaches the copy that lost a conflict.
```{r get}
data_get("counts_rna", collection = "batch2")
```

A suffix exposes every object in a collection as an alias of the form `<name><suffix>`.  Set it when you attach.  

```{r suffix}
data_attach("rnaseqBatch2", lib.loc = lib, id = "batch2", suffix = ".batch2",
            replace = TRUE)
counts_rna.batch2
```

Suffix aliases must be unique. A clash is reported when you attach, before
anything is changed. 

To clear decisions, use `data_prefer("counts_rna", NULL)`
and `data_primary(NULL)`.

## Cleaning up

```{r cleanup}
data_detach()
```

`data_detach()` removes the attached collections and the environment projectData
created, and forgets them. It does not delete files or modify objects you
already hold, so an object kept in a variable can keep reading its backing
files after detachment. That is not a promise about replacing or removing the
installed package: a disk-backed object that references installed files may stop
working then. See `?data_detach`. `data_detach("batch2")` removes just one collection. Packages you
only reached through `data_get(package = )` are forgotten the same way (they
were never on the search path); a later `data_get()` simply opens them again.

## What this does not do

* Class compatibility, software versions, backing files, and platform-specific
  readers still matter; projectData does not guarantee reproducibility.
* Returned objects are shared references to one cached resource, not
  independent copies.
* Related tools: `conflicted` resolves conflicts between package exports and
  `library(include.only = )` selects exports. They work with exported data but
  do not provide collection inventory, deferred access beyond lazy data,
  format-specific restoration, or provenance.
